title: Scheduling, Cron, and Polling Triggers
summary: Not every automation should react to an instant event - many should run on a schedule, and controlling timing precisely is a core skill. A scheduled (or cron) trigger fires at set times: every hour, every weekday at 9 AM, on the first of the month. T
content:
# Scheduling, Cron, and Polling Triggers ##### The report that arrived at 3:30 a.m. A student built a daily sales digest for a client in Mumbai. Cron set to `0 9 * * 1-5` — nine in the morning, weekdays. Tested it, worked perfectly, handed it over. The client's first message the next day: *"Why did I get the report at 3:30 in the morning?"* The workflow's time zone was UTC. `09:00 UTC` is `14:30 IST`, and the client's phone had shown the notification when it arrived in their evening, but the *data window* the script computed ("yesterday") had rolled over at a different moment than the client's day did. Two separate time-zone bugs stacked on top of each other in one small automation. Scheduling looks like the simplest topic in automation. It is quietly one of the most error-prone, because you are reasoning about time in at least three places at once: when the job fires, what window of data it covers, and which clock the human reading it uses. ##### Why scheduled automations exist Not everything should be instant. Scheduled triggers are the right choice when: - **Nobody is waiting.** A daily summary does not need to be computed at 3 a.m. the moment the last order lands. - **The source has no webhook.** Many APIs simply do not push; you must ask. - **You want to batch.** One API call fetching 500 records is far cheaper than 500 webhook-triggered runs. - **The work is inherently periodic.** Invoices on the 1st, payroll on the 25th, weekly reports on Monday. - **You want to smooth load.** Processing at 2 a.m. avoids competing with daytime traffic and rate limits. ##### Schedule triggers across the three platforms **Zapier — Schedule by Zapier.** A trigger app with friendly options: Every Hour, Every Day (pick the hour, optionally weekdays only), Every Week (pick the day), Every Month (pick the date). No raw cron. Your account time zone governs it. Simple, limited, adequate for most business schedules. **Make.com — scenario scheduling.** Click the clock on the trigger module. Options: Immediately (webhooks), Every N minutes (1 minute minimum on paid plans, 15 on free), Once, Every day, Days of the week, Days of the month, plus an **Advanced** mode that accepts real cron expressions. You can also define restricted time windows — "every 5 minutes, but only between 09:00 and 18:00 on weekdays" — which is an excellent way to cut operation consumption by two thirds. **n8n — Schedule Trigger node.** The most flexible: interval-based (seconds/minutes/hours/days), specific times, or **Custom (Cron)** with a full expression. The instance-wide time zone comes from `GENERIC_TIMEZONE`, and each workflow can override it in settings. ##### Cron expression syntax Cron comes from Unix and has been the standard way to express recurring schedules for fifty years. The classic form is five fields: ```text ┌───────────── minute (0 - 59) │ ┌─────────── hour (0 - 23) │ │ ┌───────── day of month (1 - 31) │ │ │ ┌─────── month (1 - 12) │ │ │ │ ┌───── day of week (0 - 6, Sunday = 0) │ │ │ │ │ * * * * * ``` Some implementations (including the `node-cron` library that underpins several JavaScript schedulers, and n8n) accept an optional **sixth field at the front** for seconds. The four operators do everything: | Operator | Meaning | Example | |---|---|---| | `*` | every value | `* * * * *` = every minute | | `,` | list | `0 9,13,17 * * *` = 9 AM, 1 PM, 5 PM | | `-` | range | `0 9 * * 1-5` = 9 AM Monday–Friday | | `/` | step | `*/15 * * * *` = every 15 minutes | Five expressions worth memorizing — and these are exactly what today's assignment asks you to write out: ```text */15 * * * * Every 15 minutes, all day, every day 0 * * * * Every hour, on the hour 0 9 * * 1-5 At 9:00 AM, Monday through Friday 0 8 * * 1 At 8:00 AM every Monday 30 23 L * * At 11:30 PM on the last day of the month (L is an extension; portable version: 0 0 1 * * = 1st at midnight) ``` A classic trap: **day-of-month and day-of-week are OR'd, not AND'd.** `0 9 13 * 5` means "9 AM on the 13th of any month **or** any Friday" — not "Friday the 13th." If you need both conditions, filter inside the workflow. Another: `*/7 * * * *` does not mean "every 7 minutes forever." It means minutes 0, 7, 14, 21, 28, 35, 42, 49, 56 — then the hour resets and there is only a 4-minute gap. Steps that do not divide evenly into 60 produce irregular intervals. When in doubt, paste your expression into crontab.guru; it renders a plain-English description instantly. ##### Polling intervals and their trade-offs A **polling trigger** is a scheduled check: "has anything new appeared?" The interval you choose is a genuine engineering trade-off, and the assignment asks you to reason about it. | | 1-minute polling | 15-minute polling | |---|---|---| | Worst-case delay | 1 min | 15 min | | API calls/day (per source) | 1,440 | 96 | | Platform cost | 15× higher | Baseline | | Rate-limit risk | High | Low | | Empty checks | ~95%+ typically | Fewer, denser batches | | Right for | Payments, support tickets, alerts | Reports, syncs, backups | The framing that makes the decision easy: **what does a minute of delay cost?** For a customer support ticket where response time drives satisfaction, a lot. For a nightly inventory reconciliation, nothing at all. Do not buy latency you have no use for — you pay for it in quota, cost and rate-limit headroom. And the meta-answer: **if the source supports webhooks, use them instead.** Webhooks give you sub-second latency at one request per real event — strictly better than any polling interval on both axes. Polling is what you do when push is unavailable. ```mermaid flowchart TD A[Need to detect an event] --> B{Does the source
support webhooks?} B -->|Yes| C[Use a webhook
instant, cheapest] B -->|No| D{Does a minute of
delay actually cost anything?} D -->|Yes — money or SLA| E[Poll every 1-5 min
accept the cost] D -->|No| F{Can the work be batched?} F -->|Yes| G[Scheduled batch
hourly or daily] F -->|No| H[Poll every 15-30 min] ``` ##### Time zones in scheduling Three separate clocks can disagree, and you must pin all three. **1. The platform's clock.** Zapier uses your account time zone; Make uses the organization setting; n8n uses `GENERIC_TIMEZONE` (set it to `Asia/Kolkata`) with a per-workflow override. If you never set it, assume UTC — and IST is UTC+5:30, so every schedule is off by five and a half hours. **2. The data window's clock.** "Yesterday's records" means midnight to midnight in *someone's* time zone. Compute the boundaries explicitly rather than relying on a default: ```javascript // n8n Code node: yesterday's window in IST, expressed as ISO with offset const { DateTime } = require('luxon'); // available in n8n expressions as $now const zone = 'Asia/Kolkata'; const start = DateTime.now().setZone(zone).minus({ days: 1 }).startOf('day'); const end = start.endOf('day'); return [{ json: { window_start: start.toISO(), // 2026-03-13T00:00:00.000+05:30 window_end: end.toISO(), // 2026-03-13T23:59:59.999+05:30 label: start.toFormat('dd LLL yyyy'), }, }]; ``` **3. The reader's clock.** Format timestamps in the recipient's local time in the message body. A report for a Mumbai team should read `14 Mar 2026, 9:00 AM IST`, not a raw UTC string. Add **daylight saving** to the list if any party is in Europe or North America. `0 9 * * *` in `America/New_York` fires at 13:00 UTC for half the year and 14:00 UTC for the other half — which is correct behaviour, but it will surprise you if you assumed a fixed offset. India has no DST, which is one small mercy. ##### Batch versus real-time processing Scheduling is really a choice of processing *style*, and it is worth naming the trade-offs explicitly. **Real-time (event-driven)** — webhook fires, one record processed immediately. - Wins: minimal latency, natural for user-facing actions, load is spread evenly. - Costs: one platform run per event (expensive at high volume), harder to reason about ordering, no natural place to do cross-record work. **Batch (scheduled)** — collect many records, process them together on a timer. - Wins: dramatically cheaper per record, allows aggregation and deduplication across the batch, easier to retry as a unit, fewer API calls via bulk endpoints. - Costs: latency equal to the interval, a failure can affect the whole batch, and a large batch can hit timeouts. Many mature systems use **both**: a webhook handles the urgent, user-visible slice ("confirm the order immediately"), while a nightly batch handles the heavy, tolerant slice ("reconcile inventory, refresh the warehouse, rebuild the report"). Choosing per-use-case rather than per-project is the mark of good design. ##### Common pitfalls - **Unset time zone** — the 3:30 a.m. report. - **Overlapping runs.** A job scheduled every 5 minutes that takes 7 minutes will run concurrently with itself, causing duplicate processing. Either shorten the job, lengthen the interval, or add a "run in progress" lock flag. - **Assuming exact firing times.** Platforms queue jobs; a 9:00 schedule may fire at 9:00:47. Never build logic that depends on second-level precision. - **Data windows that drift.** If your job says "records from the last 24 hours" and the run is delayed, you create a gap. Use explicit boundaries or a stored `last_run_at` watermark instead. - **Polling too fast on a free plan** and silently getting throttled. - **Forgetting month-end.** `0 9 31 * *` skips February, April, June, September and November entirely. - **No empty-batch handling.** Sending "Here is your daily report: (nothing)" every Sunday looks broken. Either skip or say "no activity." ##### Your hands-on tie-in The practical task: build a **scheduled automation that runs every weekday morning**, pulls yesterday's records from a sheet or API, and sends a summary — with the **correct time zone** configured and a **cron expression** where the platform supports one. `0 9 * * 1-5` is your expression. Verify the time zone by scheduling a throwaway run five minutes from now and checking that it actually fires when you expect. The mini project is the **daily digest**: on a weekday-morning cron, gather new items from the past 24 hours across a couple of sources, format them into one report, and deliver by **both email and Slack**. Handle the empty case gracefully, and compute the 24-hour window explicitly rather than trusting a default. For the assignment, write your **five cron expressions in plain English** and explain the **1-minute vs 15-minute polling trade-off**. Ground the explanation in numbers — 1,440 versus 96 calls a day — and finish with the point that matters most: if a webhook is available, neither interval is the right answer. ##### Key takeaways - Scheduled triggers are for work nobody is waiting on, sources without webhooks, batchable jobs, and inherently periodic tasks. - Cron's five fields plus `* , - /` express almost any schedule; remember that day-of-month and day-of-week are OR'd, and verify with crontab.guru. - Polling interval is a latency-versus-cost trade-off — buy low latency only where delay genuinely costs something, and prefer webhooks whenever they exist. - Pin all three clocks: the platform's time zone, the data window boundaries, and the format shown to the reader. - Batch is cheaper and allows aggregation; real-time is instant and user-facing. Mature systems deliberately use both.
